Why Neil deGrasse Tyson Is Wrong About Atheism

I thought he was right. He plainly states he is more agnostic than atheist so that's why he doesn't claim to be one. Then goes on to say labels are intellectually lazy, which is what kicks off the disagreement with the author. Perhaps qualifying the statement with "can" instead of "is" would have been more appropriate. Too often people use labels to that end, so I agree with Tyson on this.

Yes, they're really talking about two different things. But I think Tyson is making a mistake calling himself agnostic (which is, after all, another label). I'd be very surprised if, when push comes to shove, he didn't agree with the statement, "There is no God as the term conventionally means in the Abrahamic religions" -- which is, for all practical purposes, the belief that the word atheist describes. I agree with this statement, and so I describe myself as an atheist even though I have concerns about the label that are similar to Tyson's.

I suspect that most people who describe themselves as agnostic are attempting to display open mindedness. But it's a false open mindedness. Open mindedness isn't the absence of an opinion, or even the absence of a strong belief. Open mindedness is simply being willing to change your opinion in the face of new evidence or new arguments. True open mindedness is only possible once you have committed to an opinion. Not having an opinion is merely not having an opinion. Not having an opinion is fine if it's a subject about which you have substantial ignorance of the evidence and arguments. But there can be few adults who can make that claim about the existence of God.

Sorry but atheism doesn't specify Abrahamic in any way. It is simply the lack of belief in the existence of any deity or deities. No more and no less. I tend to think of it as an emphatic denial (Tyson appears to tend to think of it that way too), as opposed to agnosticism which basically says "I don't have the faintest idea whether it exists or not", but to be fair, it is just the lack or absence of affirmative belief.

Neither committing to an affirmative belief, nor to a denial, can mean a lot more than just having "no opinion", as you claim. It can mean that you have carefully considered the matter and can find no proof or disproof. It can even mean that you cannot conceive of the concept that there could ever be any proof or disproof. In fact to some of us, anyone who who is NOT an agnostic appears as a presumptuous fool.

But I think Tyson is making a mistake calling himself agnostic (which is, after all, another label).

He even says, "If you require that I give myself a label then the closest word I can come up with is agnostic," ... so I don't think he really digs the label thing at all
